title: Energy bands and band gap
summary: Why solids split into conductors, semiconductors, insulators.

layers.basics: In a crystal, allowed electron energies merge into bands separated by gaps. Silicon’s gap is 1.12 eV, small enough to control electrically.
layers.deeper: A completely full valence band cannot carry net current; electrons lifted to the conduction band move freely and leave mobile holes behind.
layers.expert: E_g(Si)=1.12 eV, Ge 0.66, GaAs 1.42 (direct), SiC ≈3.0–3.3 depending on polytype (4H ≈3.2, 6H ≈3.05), GaN 3.4; intrinsic concentration nᵢ≈10¹⁰ cm⁻³ for Si at 300 K, varying roughly as T^{3/2}e^{−E_g/2kT} (E_g itself shrinks as T rises).

title: Doping: n-type and p-type material
summary: Adding impurities to set carrier type.

layers.basics: Adding a few phosphorus atoms gives free electrons (n-type); boron gives holes (p-type). Doping can change the conductivity of silicon by many orders of magnitude.
layers.deeper: Dopants of ~10¹⁵–10²⁰ cm⁻³ dominate over intrinsic carriers; in equilibrium, for non-degenerate material, the mass-action law np=nᵢ² ties electrons and holes.
layers.expert: Donor/acceptor levels sit ~45 meV from band edges for P/B in Si, essentially fully ionised at room temperature at moderate doping; at very heavy (degenerate) doping ionisation is incomplete and np=nᵢ² no longer holds; compensation also matters.

layers.basics: Carriers drift in an electric field and diffuse from high to low concentration.
layers.deeper: Electron current J_n=qnμ_nE+qD_n dn/dx and hole current J_p=qpμ_pE−qD_p dp/dx; the total is their sum. The Einstein relation links mobility and diffusion.
layers.expert: D=μkT/q (thermal voltage kT/q≈25.9 mV at 300 K); velocity saturates near 10⁷ cm/s in Si at high fields.

title: The PN junction
summary: A diode is born where n meets p.

layers.basics: Where p-type meets n-type, carriers diffuse across, leaving a depletion zone with a built-in field; this lets current pass one way only.
layers.deeper: Forward bias shrinks the barrier and current grows exponentially; reverse bias widens it and little current flows.
layers.expert: I=I_s(e^{V/nV_T}−1); built-in potential V_bi=V_T ln(N_aN_d/nᵢ²) with V_T=kT/q the thermal voltage, about 0.6 V for Si doped 10¹⁵ cm⁻³ on both sides and rising with doping (not the 0.7 V conventional forward drop); ideality n between 1 and 2.

layers.basics: Simple models: an ideal one-way switch; or a switch with a 0.7 V drop; or the full exponential curve.
layers.deeper: Load-line analysis and iterative solving give operating points; small-signal resistance r_d=nV_T/I.
layers.expert: SPICE diode includes series R_s, junction capacitance for reverse bias (V_R>0) C_j=C_j0/(1+V_R/V_bi)^m, which SPICE linearises in forward bias, and transit time for charge storage.

layers.basics: A diode lets only one half of an AC wave through. A bridge of four diodes uses both halves.
layers.deeper: A filter capacitor smooths the ripple; ripple ≈ I/(2fC) for full-wave, with f the mains frequency.
layers.expert: Half-wave: V_dc=Vm/π; full-wave: 2Vm/π ≈ 0.637 Vm, less about two diode drops in a bridge; diode peak inverse voltage and conduction angle drive transformer sizing and EMI.

layers.basics: Clippers trim peaks off a signal; clampers shift its DC level.
layers.deeper: Input protection and level shifting; a clamper holds a capacitor charged to a peak.
layers.expert: Biased clippers use reference voltages; the clamper's RC time constant must be much longer than the signal period so the capacitor does not discharge between peaks.

title: Zener diodes and regulation
summary: A diode that holds a steady reverse voltage.

layers.basics: In reverse breakdown, a zener holds nearly constant voltage, so it provides a simple voltage reference.
layers.deeper: Series resistor limits current; load and line regulation depend on dynamic resistance.
layers.expert: Breakdown below about 5.6 V is mainly the Zener (tunnelling) effect, with a negative temperature coefficient; above it avalanche dominates, with a positive coefficient. Near 5.6 V both act and the coefficients nearly cancel. Bandgap references are better.

layers.basics: In an LED, electrons and holes recombine and emit light; a photodiode does the reverse, turning light into current.
layers.deeper: LED colour is set by band gap: ~1.9 eV red, ~2.7 eV blue; limit current with a series resistor or a constant-current driver.
layers.expert: Direct band-gap materials (GaAs, GaN) radiate efficiently; photodiode in photoconductive (reverse-bias) mode is fast, and it can also run with no bias (photovoltaic mode); I_ph=ηqP/hν.

title: BJT operation and regions
summary: A transistor where a small base current goes with a much larger collector current.

layers.basics: A bipolar transistor has three layers (NPN or PNP). A small base current controls a much larger collector current.
layers.deeper: Regions: cutoff (off), active (amplifier), saturation (switch on); β=I_C/I_B is typically about 50–300 for small-signal parts and varies with current and temperature. Active region: base–emitter forward-biased, base–collector reverse-biased.
layers.expert: I_C=I_s e^{V_BE/V_T}(1+V_CE/V_A); Ebers–Moll model; transconductance g_m=I_C/V_T.

layers.basics: Resistors set the transistor’s idle currents so it works as a linear amplifier; the bias must survive temperature and β variation.
layers.deeper: Voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor is the standard stable arrangement.
layers.expert: Q-point on the load line; stability factor S=ΔI_C/ΔI_CO; emitter degeneration reduces sensitivity.

layers.basics: For small inputs the transistor behaves linearly; its model has r_π, g_m and r_o.
layers.deeper: Compute gain from the model by replacing DC sources with zero and capacitors with shorts.
layers.expert: Hybrid-π: r_π=β/g_m, r_o=V_A/I_C; T-model is alternative; high-frequency adds C_π and C_μ.

layers.basics: Common-emitter gives voltage gain and inversion; common-collector (emitter follower) buffers; common-base is fast.
layers.deeper: Choose by gain, input and output impedance. Follower: gain ≈1, high Z_in, low Z_out.
layers.expert: CE A_v≈−g_mR_C; CC A_v≈g_mR_E/(1+g_mR_E); CB Z_in≈1/g_m; cascode CE+CB improves bandwidth.

layers.basics: Driving a BJT between cutoff and saturation lets a small control signal switch a larger current.
layers.deeper: A base resistor sets drive; V_CE(sat) is typically a few tenths of a volt or less for small-signal parts, depending on I_C and base drive; a flyback diode protects against inductive loads.
layers.expert: Storage-time delay in saturation limits speed; Baker clamps reduce it by preventing deep saturation. Darlington pairs give high current gain but a higher V_CE(sat).

layers.basics: A MOSFET’s gate voltage creates a conducting channel between source and drain; almost no gate current flows.
layers.deeper: Above threshold V_T the channel forms; current grows with V_GS and saturates for high V_DS.
layers.expert: MOS capacitor regimes: accumulation, depletion, inversion; threshold V_T=V_FB+2φ_F+Q_dep/C_ox; body effect.

layers.basics: At small V_DS the MOSFET acts as a resistor; at large V_DS the current saturates.
layers.deeper: Square-law model, valid in saturation (V_DS ≥ V_GS−V_T) for a long channel: I_D=½k(V_GS−V_T)² with k=μC_ox W/L; g_m=∂I_D/∂V_GS.
layers.expert: Channel-length modulation λ; velocity saturation makes current linear in overdrive in short channels; subthreshold current exponential.

layers.basics: A resistor divider sets the gate voltage, or a current source (often a mirror) sets the drain current directly, so the MOSFET stays in saturation.
layers.deeper: Source degeneration and constant-current biasing improve stability.
layers.expert: IC design uses bias currents from mirrors and gm/Id methodology rather than hand-picked resistors.

layers.basics: Common-source gives gain; common-drain (source follower) buffers; common-gate suits high-frequency.
layers.deeper: A_v≈−g_m(r_o∥R_D) for CS; follower gain<1 and no inversion.
layers.expert: Cascode, folded cascode, and active loads raise output resistance and so gain; one transistor's intrinsic gain g_m r_o is limited by its finite r_o, and a cascode raises it towards about (g_m r_o)².

layers.basics: A MOSFET fully on acts like a small resistor R_DS(on) and off like an open circuit; it is the basis of digital logic and power converters.
layers.deeper: Switching loss comes from gate charge and overlapping V and I during transitions.
layers.expert: P_cond=I²R_DS(on); P_sw≈½V I (t_r+t_f) f_sw+Q_g V_g f_sw; body-diode recovery matters in bridges.

layers.basics: In CMOS each gate has PMOS transistors that pull the output up and NMOS that pull it down; only one network conducts at once so static power is tiny.
layers.deeper: NAND = series NMOS + parallel PMOS; NOR the opposite. Dynamic power ≈ αCV²f.
layers.expert: Noise margins, propagation delay t_p≈0.69RC, logical effort; leakage grew into a major part of chip power in deep-submicron generations; high-k gates and FinFETs reduced it, but it remains significant, especially in idle blocks.

layers.basics: Gain says how much bigger the output is; input/output impedance say how it loads and is loaded.
layers.deeper: Voltage gain in dB is 20 log₁₀|A_v| (power gain uses 10 log₁₀), so a gain of 100 is 40 dB. For a single-pole amplifier, gain × bandwidth is constant: the gain-bandwidth product.
layers.expert: Two-port model with R_in, R_out, A_v; frequency roll-off set by coupling capacitors (low) and parasitics (high).

title: Miller effect
summary: Feedback capacitance looks bigger at the input.

layers.basics: A capacitor bridging an inverting amplifier looks (1+A) times larger from the input, which cuts bandwidth.
layers.deeper: Cascodes avoid it by keeping the voltage at the amplifier’s inner node nearly constant.
layers.expert: C_M=C_μ(1+|A_v|); dominant pole f_p≈1/(2π R_s C_M); pole splitting also stabilises op-amps.

title: Differential amplifier
summary: Amplify the difference of two inputs.

layers.basics: A differential pair amplifies the difference between two inputs and rejects what both share (noise).
layers.deeper: Common-mode rejection ratio CMRR measures this; the tail current source sets the gain.
layers.expert: For a single-ended output, A_d=g_m R_D/2 and A_cm≈−R_D/(2R_tail) (taking R_tail ≫ 1/g_m), so CMRR≈g_m R_tail. For a differential output, A_d=g_m R_D and a perfectly matched pair has A_cm≈0. The long-tailed pair is the input stage of most voltage-feedback op-amps.

layers.basics: A pair of matched transistors copies a reference current to another branch.
layers.deeper: Used for bias in ICs and as active loads that give large gain.
layers.expert: Mirror error from λ and mismatch; Wilson/cascode mirrors raise output resistance.

layers.basics: A current-mirror load gives high gain in little chip area.
layers.deeper: Small-signal gain is g_m(r_on∥r_op), about g_m r_o/2 for equal r_o. The mirror also converts the differential signal to a single-ended output.
layers.expert: Output resistance r_o∥r_o; limits of headroom; common-mode feedback required in fully differential stages.

layers.basics: Stages are chained for more gain, with input, gain and output stages.
layers.deeper: Gain multiplies, bandwidth shrinks, loading between stages matters.
layers.expert: Two-stage Miller-compensated op-amp is the textbook design; for n identical, non-interacting single-pole stages the overall bandwidth is √(2^{1/n}−1) times that of one stage.

title: Output stages (Class A, B, AB, D)

layers.basics: Class A conducts all the time (clean, wasteful); class B splits the wave between two transistors; AB adds bias to avoid crossover distortion; D switches fully on/off.
layers.deeper: Maximum theoretical efficiency with a sine wave: class A 25% (50% with inductive or transformer coupling), class B 78.5%. Class D above 80% is common and above 90% is achievable.
layers.expert: Class D PWM + LC filter; the switching frequency is at least about ten times the highest audio frequency, typically hundreds of kHz; thermal design; a Vbe-multiplier bias reduces crossover distortion by setting a small quiescent current.

title: Ideal op-amp
summary: A high-gain amplifier with two golden rules.

layers.basics: With negative feedback, an op-amp adjusts its output so its two inputs are at the same voltage and draw no current.
layers.deeper: Infinite gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance: analysis becomes simple algebra.
layers.expert: Virtual short and zero input current; A_OL≈10⁵–10⁶ gives closed-loop gain 1/β.

layers.basics: Feed the input through a resistor to the − terminal and connect Rf from output back; the output is an inverted, scaled copy.
layers.deeper: Virtual ground at the − input makes input impedance equal Rin.
layers.expert: Closed-loop BW=GBW/(1+Rf/Rin); noise gain 1+Rf/Rin.

layers.basics: Input goes to the + terminal and feedback divides output to the − terminal; gain is at least 1, input impedance very high.
layers.deeper: The voltage follower (gain 1) buffers a source.
layers.expert: BW=GBW/(1+Rf/Rg); input impedance boosted by loop gain.

layers.basics: Several inputs through resistors into the inverting node give an output that is their weighted sum, inverted.
layers.deeper: Basis of a simple DAC and audio mixer.
layers.expert: Vout=−Rf Σ(Vi/Ri); inputs are isolated by virtual ground.

title: Op-amp integrator
summary: Output is the integral of the input.

layers.basics: Replacing Rf with a capacitor makes the output the running integral of the input.
layers.deeper: Used in analog computing, ramp generators and ADCs; needs a reset or drift resistor.
layers.expert: H(s)=−1/(sRC); DC offset leads to saturation without a high-value feedback resistor.

title: Op-amp differentiator
summary: Output is the derivative of the input.

layers.basics: Swapping R and C yields an output proportional to the input’s slope; amplifies high-frequency noise.
layers.deeper: Practical versions add a series resistor to cap the high-frequency gain.
layers.expert: H(s)=−sRC; stability needs a pole to limit loop gain.

title: Instrumentation amplifier
summary: Precise amplification of small differential signals.

layers.basics: Three op-amps and a gain resistor amplify the tiny difference from sensors like bridges and ECG electrodes, with high input impedance and CMRR.
layers.deeper: One resistor sets the gain, and matched resistors determine CMRR.
layers.expert: for the three-op-amp topology with a unity-gain difference stage, G=1+2R/R_G; good ICs can exceed 100 dB CMRR at higher gain settings, and CMRR falls with frequency; chopper stabilisation cancels offset.

layers.basics: A comparator outputs high or low depending on which input is greater; it is a 1-bit ADC.
layers.deeper: It uses no feedback or positive feedback; noise at the threshold causes chatter.
layers.expert: Propagation delay, overdrive, input offset, open-collector vs push-pull outputs.

layers.basics: Positive feedback creates two thresholds so noise does not cause chatter.
layers.deeper: Used for debouncing and cleaning slow edges into clean logic.
layers.expert: V_T±=±V_sat R₁/(R₁+R₂); hysteresis width = 2V_sat R₁/(R₁+R₂).

layers.basics: Real op-amps have offset voltage, finite speed and finite gain; these limit accuracy and bandwidth.
layers.deeper: Slew rate SR limits large signals: full-power bandwidth f=SR/(2πV_p); GBW fixes small-signal bandwidth.
layers.expert: Bias current, offset drift, CMRR, PSRR, input noise density (nV/√Hz), output swing; rule: closed-loop BW=GBW/noise gain.

layers.basics: Feeding part of the output back to subtract from the input makes the gain predictable and cuts distortion.
layers.deeper: Four topologies (series/shunt, voltage/current) change input and output impedances.
layers.expert: A_f=A/(1+Aβ); desensitivity; for a single-pole amplifier the closed-loop bandwidth is (1+Aβ) times the open-loop bandwidth, and distortion within the loop is reduced by about the same factor, where the loop gain is large.

layers.basics: If the loop gain reaches 1 at a frequency where the phase has swung 180°, a feedback amplifier oscillates; margins measure how far from this we are.
layers.deeper: Phase margin >45° (60° preferred) is the rule of thumb for a well-damped step response.
layers.expert: PM=180°+∠L(jω_c); GM=−20log|L(jω_180)|; compensation by dominant pole or lead networks.

layers.basics: An oscillator is an amplifier whose output is fed back with exactly the right phase and gain to sustain a sine wave.
layers.deeper: Barkhausen criterion: loop gain 1 and phase 0°. Wien bridge uses RC; Colpitts uses LC; crystals give accurate frequency.
layers.expert: Wien: f=1/2πRC with gain 3; Colpitts f=1/2π√(L C₁C₂/(C₁+C₂)); quartz Q≈10⁴–10⁶, with stability of ppm order that depends on cut, temperature and ageing (oven control improves it); amplitude limited by non-linearity.

layers.basics: Op-amps with RC networks make filters without inductors, with gain and sharp responses.
layers.deeper: Sallen–Key and multiple-feedback second-order sections cascade into higher orders.
layers.expert: Butterworth maximally flat, Chebyshev ripple for sharper edge, Bessel linear phase; Q set by component ratios and op-amp GBW.

title: Analog-to-digital converters
summary: Measuring a voltage as a number.

layers.basics: An ADC samples a voltage and turns it into a binary number; more bits, finer steps.
layers.deeper: Architectures: flash (fast), SAR (balanced), sigma-delta (precise), pipeline.
layers.expert: LSB=V_FS/2ᴺ with V_FS the full-scale range (V_ref for a unipolar converter); ideal SNR=6.02N+1.76 dB; INL/DNL; aperture jitter limits SNR at high input frequency; plain oversampling gains 3 dB per octave of oversampling; sigma-delta noise shaping gains (6L+3) dB per octave for an order-L modulator.

formula: SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB (ideal N-bit, full-scale sine, quantisation noise only)

layers.basics: A DAC converts a binary code into a voltage or current using a weighted network of resistors or capacitors.
layers.deeper: R-2R ladders give accurate binary weighting; PWM plus a filter is a cheap DAC.
layers.expert: Settling time, glitch energy, DNL; reconstruction filter removes images; sigma-delta DACs use noise shaping.

title: Linear regulators (LDO)
summary: Steady voltage by burning the excess.

layers.basics: A linear regulator uses a pass transistor and feedback to hold a fixed output; the excess voltage is dissipated as heat.
layers.deeper: Dropout is the smallest V_in − V_out at which the output still regulates; low-dropout (LDO) regulators work close to the input voltage; low noise makes them good for analog.
layers.expert: Dropout, PSRR, quiescent current, stability with output-cap ESR; P_diss≈(Vin−Vout)·I_load + Vin·I_q, where I_q is the quiescent (ground-pin) current.
